title: CFA Ethics 20: Mosaic theory - the line between excellent analysis and insider dealing
subtitle: Why assembling many non-material pieces is lawful, while a single material one is not
whyItMatters: This is the concept that protects the analyst's job itself: if assembling public information into a superior conclusion were also banned, there would be no reason left to do research. But the line is narrow, and the exam attacks exactly the narrow part.
openingQuestion: You interview ten suppliers of a retailer, each speaking only about their own orders. Putting it together, you conclude this quarter's revenue will fall sharply and you sell the stock before the company announces. Is this insider dealing?
openingOptions: Yes, because you know the outcome before the market knows it
No, provided each individual piece was not material on its own
Yes, because you dealt directly with parties connected to the company
No, because information from suppliers is never counted as material
explanation: Mosaic theory says that a material conclusion produced by assembling pieces that are neither material nor inside information is the lawful property of the analyst who assembled it. The logic behind it is direct: ban this and the reward for doing research disappears, and the market loses the very mechanism that puts information into prices. The line sits in three questions. Was each piece material - if one supplier tells you the unpublished revenue total, that piece is already material. Was the source under a duty of confidentiality - if the person speaking is breaching their own duty, you are not clean merely because you were the listener. And did you know that.

summary.keyIdea: Assembling many NON-material pieces into a material conclusion is lawful, and that is precisely where the value of analysis lies.
summary.commonMistake: Confusing a mosaic with taking one material unpublished piece and wrapping it in a lot of public ones. A material piece does not become clean by being placed next to nine clean ones.

application.title: Where the line sits
application.message: Ask: if this one piece were removed, would the conclusion still stand? If it would not, that piece is the material one.

sections.text: Mosaic theory is the line between outstanding analysis and insider dealing - and it sits in the inputs, not in the conclusion that comes out.

A material conclusion produced by assembling many public or non-material pieces of information is the lawful property of the analyst. The logic behind it is direct: ban this and the reward for doing research disappears, and the market loses the very mechanism that puts information into prices.

sections.label: A material conclusion is the goal, not the problem
sections.text: What has to be examined is never whether your conclusion is important - it is where each input piece came from.
Three questions that fix the line

items: Was each piece material? If a supplier gives you the unpublished revenue total, that piece is already material and the whole chain is broken.
Was the source under a duty of confidentiality? If the person speaking is breaching their own duty, you are not clean merely because you were the listener.
Did you know that? Knowing, or having had reason to know, leads to the same conclusion.

sections.text: What distinguishes a genuine mosaic argument from an excuse when the question is asked later is the record: note the source of each piece, the date it was obtained, and how the pieces were assembled into the conclusion. Without a record, the two cases look identical from the outside.

left.label: A lawful mosaic
left.text: You call 12 suppliers to an electronics maker. Each speaks about THEIR OWN orders this quarter - their information, not material to the market when it stands alone. Eleven of them say orders are down. You put it together and conclude the maker's revenue will fall short of the consensus forecast. That conclusion is highly material, and it is entirely your property - because the work of assembling the pieces was yours.

right.label: A contaminated chain
right.text: In those 12 calls, one supplier says: "They have just told us this quarter will fall short of forecast." That piece is the company's own material non-public information, passed through a third party. From the moment you hear it, the whole analytical chain is contaminated - and the fact that you already held the other 11 legitimate pieces does not wash it out.

sections.label: The record is what separates a real argument from an excuse
sections.text: The two situations above look identical from the outside: the same analyst, the same conclusion, the same trade order. The only thing that tells them apart when the question is asked two years later is the research file - the source of each piece, the date it was obtained, and the reasoning linking the pieces together. Without that file, mosaic theory is not a defence, it is just a sentence. This is why large institutions require call notes to be recorded on the day, rather than when somebody asks.

lines: The raw material that produced it may not be.

The source breaches no duty of confidentiality

realWorldExample.company: Why record-keeping is the most important part of a mosaic
realWorldExample.description: When a regulator reviews a highly profitable trade placed just before bad news, the question they ask is how you knew. Without a file, the explanation "I worked it out myself" cannot be distinguished from an excuse. With a file - interview notes, dates, the public sources read, drafts of the reasoning - that documentary chain is itself the evidence for the mosaic. This is why Standard V(C) on record retention is bound far more tightly to Standard II(A) in practice than it is on paper.

quiz.question: What does mosaic theory protect?
options: The right to use a conclusion built from non-material pieces
The right to use inside information if it serves research purposes
The right to publish material information before the company does
The right to keep your analytical method secret from regulators
quiz.explanation: Without this principle every superior conclusion would be suspect, and investment research would lose its whole economic motive. The inside-information answer inverts the doctrine: mosaic theory exists because the pieces were not inside information, so a research purpose cannot launder a piece that was. Publishing material information ahead of the issuer is a separate breach regardless of how the information was assembled. And nothing in mosaic theory shields a method from a regulator - the opposite is true, since the research file is what proves the mosaic was real.

quiz.question: What destroys the lawfulness of a mosaic?
options: That the final conclusion turns out material to the whole market
One of the pieces in it is material non-public information
That you were in direct contact with the company's staff
That you traded ahead of publishing your research report
quiz.explanation: A material conclusion is the goal, not the problem. The problem lies in the inputs: one material unpublished piece ruins the entire chain. Direct contact with company staff is ordinary analytical work and breaks nothing on its own - what matters is what was said, not that a conversation happened. Trading ahead of your own published report engages a different duty entirely, the priority of client transactions, and it can be a breach without any mosaic question arising. Only the input test decides whether the assembly itself was lawful.

quiz.question: What if your source is breaching their own duty of confidentiality?
options: You only breach this if you paid to obtain the information
You are clear: that duty is between them and their employer
You are not clean merely because you listened rather than spoke
You are clear if you republish the information publicly now
quiz.explanation: The decisive element is that you knew, or were bound to know, that the source was in breach. That awareness pulls you into the chain of responsibility. Payment is not what creates the liability - it may be evidence of an inducement, but the duty attaches to the knowledge, not the invoice. Treating the duty as purely the source's own affair ignores that the tippee doctrine exists precisely to reach the listener. And republishing the information does not cure it either; broadcasting someone else's confidential information is an additional breach rather than a remedy.

quiz.question: Why does keeping a research file matter so much for a mosaic?
options: Because Standard II(A) sets the retention period for research files
Because regulators require files to be filed before every large trade
Because the file lets colleagues reuse the research results later on
Because it is the evidence separating real analysis from a denial
quiz.explanation: Without a file, the explanation "I worked it out myself" sounds exactly like an excuse. The documentary chain is the mosaic, proven. The Standard II(A) answer swaps the standards around: retention sits in Standard V(C), while II(A) governs material non-public information. Nobody files research with a regulator before a trade - the file is kept internally and produced only if the trade is later reviewed. And reuse by colleagues is a genuine benefit of good notes, but it is an efficiency, not the reason the record is what makes the defence stand up.

quiz.question: What should an investor who receives material non-public information by accident do?
options: Do not trade, and tell the firm's compliance department about it
Trade as normal, since you did not seek the information out
Pass it on to the largest clients so everyone is treated fairly
Wait a full 24 hours and then trade, since the news is stale
quiz.explanation: How the information was obtained does not matter - the duty arises from the fact that you now hold it. Passing it on is a separate violation of its own. That is why the fairness answer fails: telling some clients is selective disclosure, which widens the breach rather than curing it. Trading anyway because the information arrived unsought reads intent into a rule that turns on possession. And waiting a fixed period does nothing, because information becomes stale only when the market has it, which requires the issuer to publish, not a clock to run.

keyTakeaways: Assembling non-material pieces into a material conclusion is lawful and is your property
One material unpublished piece ruins the whole chain
If the source breaches a duty of confidentiality, the listener is pulled in too
A material conclusion is the goal, not the problem - the inputs are what get examined
The record is what separates a mosaic from an excuse when the question is asked later

practicePrompt.question: An airline employee tells you the airport has been unusually quiet this month. You combine it with public fare data and sell airline stocks. Assessment?
options: A violation, because you got information from an industry insider
A valid mosaic: airport traffic is not inside information at all
A violation, because you traded before publishing your analysis
Valid only if you disclose the source of the tip in your report
practicePrompt.explanation: Run the three questions: is this piece material non-public information about a specific company - no, it is a general observation about the sector; is the source breaching a duty of confidentiality - no, airport footfall is not any carrier's trade secret; do you know of any breach - there is no breach to know of. The first option is the most common misunderstanding: talking to people in an industry is exactly what an analyst's job consists of.
